programme_transition.transfer_summary: Your Sociology studies introduce you to analysing social structures and society's dynamics, using ideas about culture and socialisation, and examining human behaviour. These are relevant starting points for Social Sciences-not the whole set of capabilities used across the field. Beyond the programme, the path shows shared domain foundations, optional useful edges, and additions for the areas or roles you choose. It does not claim every employer requires every item or that your degree already taught these additions.
programme_transition.transferable_learning_summary: Analysing social structures and societal dynamics; using core ideas about culture and socialisation; examining human behaviour.

aggregate_count_audit.learner_display_policy: Do not display aggregate counts; use only individually resolved course/outcome evidence and its explanation.

programme_transition.domain_overview: Social Sciences helps you understand how people live together, how groups and institutions shape everyday life, and how societies change. It connects questions about culture, family, work, inequality, crime, policy and community life to evidence gathered through research. The field looks at individual behaviour as well as the relationships between people, institutions, the environment and wider social systems. Different disciplines study these questions from different viewpoints: Sociology is one route into Social Sciences, not another name for the whole field. In Nigeria, the NUC places Sociology alongside programmes such as Economics, Political Science and Psychology within Social Sciences. Researchers use concepts, comparison and evidence to describe patterns, examine explanations and consider social responses. What a particular study can conclude depends on its question, evidence and method.
programme_transition.transition_policy: Show all programme themes and their outcomes together at the programme level. At the domain transition, carry only explicit, source-matched course/outcome context as prior learning; distinguish it from the additional domain foundations and optional route learning. Curriculum connections are not claims of mastery.

src:manchester-social-network-analysis.title: University of Manchester: Social Network Analysis
src:manchester-social-network-analysis.supports: SNA studies relations among actors/nodes, ties/edges and actor attributes; provides method-specific introductory explanation.
src:manchester-social-network-analysis.limits: An introductory methods page; it does not establish SNA as necessary for every sociology or D078 route.

src:columbia-social-network-analysis.title: Columbia University: Social Network Analysis
src:columbia-social-network-analysis.supports: Distinction between attribute and relational data, network boundaries, graph representations, and examples of network measures.
src:columbia-social-network-analysis.limits: Population-health examples; measures and interpretation must be selected for the social-science question and data quality.

src:networkx-social-analysis-learning.title: NetworkX Guides: Facebook Network Analysis
src:networkx-social-analysis-learning.supports: Free applied tutorial showing a social-network dataset represented and analysed with NetworkX.
src:networkx-social-analysis-learning.limits: A Facebook friend-network example; not a general sampling/ethics guide and not transferable as a claim about other populations.

src:networkx-official-tutorial.title: NetworkX official tutorial
src:networkx-official-tutorial.supports: Official reference for representing graph nodes/edges, attributes and basic graph operations; appropriate as a tool learning resource after the method is chosen.
src:networkx-official-tutorial.limits: Software documentation teaches implementation, not sound social-network research design, data collection or ethical practice.

src:mixed-methods-designs.title: Fetters, Curry & Creswell: Achieving Integration in Mixed Methods Designs
src:mixed-methods-designs.supports: Exploratory sequential, explanatory sequential and convergent mixed-method designs; integration must be planned across design, methods and interpretation.
src:mixed-methods-designs.limits: Methods paper, with health-care examples; it supports design logic, not a claim that every D078 task needs mixed methods.

src:questionnaire-development-qualitativ.title: Selecting, Designing, and Developing Your Questionnaire
src:questionnaire-development-qualitativ.supports: Qualitative exploration, including focus groups, can inform questionnaire concepts and response ranges; surveys are not suitable for every question.
src:questionnaire-development-qualitativ.limits: Questionnaire-development guidance; it does not make focus groups mandatory before every survey.

src:survey-questionnaire-development.title: Developing Questionnaires for Educational Research: AMEE Guide No. 87
src:survey-questionnaire-development.supports: Interview/focus-group input, cognitive interviews and pilot testing as possible questionnaire development stages.
src:survey-questionnaire-development.limits: Education/health research guidance; transfer the method logic, not domain-specific requirements.

src:survey-mixed-methods.title: Mixed Methods and Survey Research in Family Medicine and Community Health
src:survey-mixed-methods.supports: Surveys can precede qualitative follow-up, follow qualitative exploration, or be compared with concurrent qualitative evidence in mixed-method designs.
src:survey-mixed-methods.limits: Health/community examples; does not establish that any particular social-science study needs both.

src:case-study-multiple-evidence.title: The Case Study Approach
src:case-study-multiple-evidence.supports: Case studies may combine questionnaires, interviews, focus groups and observation as multiple sources of evidence.
src:case-study-multiple-evidence.limits: Health-services examples; the evidence-source logic is general but not a universal recipe.

src:case-study-research-guide.title: Case studies: a guide for researchers, educators, and implementers
src:case-study-research-guide.supports: A bounded case can use documents, interviews, ethnographic observation, focus groups and quantitative data; source choice follows the case question.
src:case-study-research-guide.limits: Practical guide; it does not imply all sources must be collected in every case study.

src:document-elicitation-interviews.title: Participant-created documents as an elicitation tool
src:document-elicitation-interviews.supports: Documents can prompt interviews in which authors explain the meaning and context of their records.
src:document-elicitation-interviews.limits: Illustrative qualitative technique; it is conditional on suitable documents, consent and a relevant question.

src:participatory-route-area-evidence.title: D078 area/role task set and route crosswalk
src:participatory-route-area-evidence.supports: D078 task routes for participatory/action research, citizen participation, community evidence and evaluation.
src:participatory-route-area-evidence.limits: Local reviewed task-route evidence; not a universal requirement or proof that a particular method combination is appropriate.

src:ukri-research-data-policy-2026.title: UKRI Research Data Policy
src:ukri-research-data-policy-2026.supports: Research data are information collected, created, generated, observed or derived from existing sources through any research method; supports data-care preparation when a selected project handles such data.
src:ukri-research-data-policy-2026.locator: Policy statement and definition of research data
src:ukri-research-data-policy-2026.limits: A general policy, not a claim that every project must publicly share data or use the same management plan.

src:esrc-ethics-principles.title: ESRC Framework for Research Ethics: Core Principles
src:esrc-ethics-principles.supports: Ethical reflection applies across a research lifecycle; specific participant, privacy, harm and governance duties depend on the project and method.
src:esrc-ethics-principles.limits: Does not make every method ethically identical or establish a universal method prerequisite.

src:uk-data-service-qualitative-reuse.title: UK Data Service: Qualitative Data and Reuse
src:uk-data-service-qualitative-reuse.supports: Existing qualitative records such as interview transcripts, diaries, field notes and open-ended responses can be reused; qualitative and quantitative evidence can also be combined where justified.
src:uk-data-service-qualitative-reuse.locator: Qualitative data and Reusing qualitative data sections
src:uk-data-service-qualitative-reuse.limits: Reuse depends on data access, consent, context, documentation and fit to the new question.

src:uk-data-service-secondary-analysis.title: UK Data Service: New to Using Data
src:uk-data-service-secondary-analysis.supports: Secondary analysis reuses previously collected qualitative or quantitative data for a new question; social-science datasets are gathered using a range of methods.
src:uk-data-service-secondary-analysis.locator: Secondary analysis and types of social-science data sections
src:uk-data-service-secondary-analysis.limits: A new question still requires checking data provenance, access permissions, population/period coverage, measures and original collection context.

src:abm-empirical-social-research.title: Bruch and Atwell: Agent-Based Models in Empirical Social Research
src:abm-empirical-social-research.supports: Empirical social ABM can use behavioral/population evidence and requires justified model construction, evaluation, sensitivity analysis and careful interpretation of fit.
src:abm-empirical-social-research.locator: Abstract; model construction and empirical grounding; model evaluation and sensitivity analysis sections
src:abm-empirical-social-research.limits: Empirical grounding and validation are design-dependent; abstract/theoretical ABMs must not be represented as population prediction.

src:comses-odd-standards.title: CoMSES Net: Agent-Based Model Documentation Standards
src:comses-odd-standards.supports: The ODD protocol documents an agent-based model's overview, design concepts and implementation details to make models understandable and reusable.
src:comses-odd-standards.locator: Standards > Documentation Standards > The ODD Protocol
src:comses-odd-standards.limits: Documentation guidance, not a guarantee that a model is valid or empirically representative.

method_combination_selection_contract.multi_selection_policy: Never project the union of independently selected methods. Resolve the complete selected set to exact named design(s); if several designs match, require a design choice. Incomplete larger designs and unsupported sets have no combined downstream.
method_combination_selection_contract.single_selection_policy: One selected method projects only its own route; no combined design is required or implied.
method_combination_selection_contract.dominance_policy: Method contribution may be asymmetric. Keep each component's contribution explicit; do not require equal weighting or use dominance to expand into areas/roles without route evidence.

typed_relationship_edges.explanation: Use after choosing a quantitative analysis; select plausible alternative assumptions or analytic decisions that could affect the result.
Sensitivity checks are a useful extension when causal estimates depend on contestable assumptions or analysis choices.
Documented sensitivity checks can show whether exploratory synthetic-response results change under plausible analytic choices. They do not validate simulated responses as population evidence.
Scenario analysis compares plausible futures without generated personas. Use it when the question concerns future conditions rather than simulated individual responses.
Mesa and NetLogo are different agent-based modelling environments. Choose one according to the model, programming workflow and learning goal.
NetLogo is a general-purpose multi-agent modelling environment; Casevo is a narrower cognitive-agent workflow.
NetworkX and R/igraph can both support network analysis; choose based on data, required measures, language and workflow.
Gephi and R/igraph are distinct network analysis/visualisation workflows. Choose according to the analysis and communication task.

For sparse categorical-count tables, choose the exact or justified resampling procedure when the large-sample chi-square approximation is unsuitable. The tests have different reference distributions and sampling assumptions.

For independent-binomial 2×2 data, Barnard's unconditional test is an exact alternative when conditioning on both margins is not required. Its an extra unknown value the test has to account for method, variance choice and sampling assumptions differ from Fisher's conditional exact test.

For independent-binomial 2×2 data, Boschloo's unconditional test is an exact alternative based on Fisher's p-value and may be more powerful. State the sampling assumptions and two-sided p-value convention.
For a two-group independent or paired contrast, a rank-based procedure may fit the outcome/design better. It targets a rank/distribution contrast and is not a drop-in mean test.

For independent groups, a rank-based overall alternative may fit when the inferential target is a distribution/location contrast rather than group means. Use a design-matched model when covariates or complex structure matter.

For complete matched blocks with one observation per condition, a rank-based repeated comparison can be an alternative to an appropriate repeated-measures ANOVA. It does not handle every unbalanced or incomplete design.
Probit and logit are alternative link functions for a binomial model of a binary outcome. Compare fit and predicted probabilities/marginal effects rather than raw coefficient scales.

For a prediction/classification goal, tree ensembles can compete with logistic regression as predictive models. Logistic regression remains a distinct inferential GLM and neither model establishes a causal effect.

For the same association question, use Spearman for ordinal/rank or monotonic association where Pearson's linear quantitative association is not the target. Related but distinct coefficients answer different questions.
For the same association question, Kendall is a rank-based alternative when concordance, ordinal measurement or tie handling better fits than Pearson's linear association.
Choose between rank coefficients by the result you set out to estimate, tie pattern, sample and inferential procedure; Kendall tau and Spearman rho are related but not numerically interchangeable.

For high-dimensional or prediction-focused work with collinearity, penalized regression can stabilize or select coefficients relative to OLS. Shrinkage changes estimation and interpretation, so this is a conditional specialist extension rather than a default replacement.

For continuous-outcome prediction, compare nonlinear tree ensembles with a linear baseline on kept-back test data data. The choice is goal- and validation-dependent and neither model is causal by itself.

Count regression provides an outcome-distribution-based inferential model; ML regressors may be compared for prediction but are not direct substitutes for its rate interpretation or inferential the result you set out to estimate.

For prediction/classification tasks, logistic regression can be a transparent statistical baseline beside more flexible supervised models. It is also an inferential generalized linear model. The goals and interpretations differ, so this is not a one-to-one equivalence.

When exploratory evidence suggests a measurement structure, CFA can test a theory-specified structure on suitable independent or kept-back test data evidence. Do not present this as an automatic step or reuse the same data without disclosing it.
Reliability estimates complement a specified measurement model. The coefficient and assumptions must match the scale structure, and reliability is not construct validity.
Reliability estimation complements dimensionality exploration but does not establish that the scale is unidimensional or valid.

IRT and CFA can address measurement structure and comparability through different model frameworks. Choose according to item response format, the result you set out to estimate, sample and assumptions rather than treating scores as equivalent.
ERGMs are a model-based extension for theory-driven inference about tie formation and network dependence. They require network-specific foundations and model diagnostics.
Spatial association analysis builds on defining units and a defensible spatial-weights structure. It describes clustering and dependence, not a causal mechanism.
Spatial lag/error models extend regression to specified spatial dependence and weighting structures. Diagnostics guide model assessment but do not mechanically choose a model.
Moran diagnostics and spatial regression may be used together to examine spatial dependence, but a significant statistic is not an automatic model-selection rule.
The ODD protocol supports transparent ABM specification and reproducibility; it documents a model but does not validate it.
This survey-specific application uses ML response models or ensembles for nonresponse adjustment. Survey design, weighting, variance and bias assessment remain essential.
LLM-based construct measurement is a newer text-as-data technique. Validate construct meaning, scoring stability and subgroup errors against credible references.
CA analyzes sequential interaction and participants’ displayed orientations; CDA examines discourse in relation to social practices and power. They can inform one study but are not interchangeable.
Process tracing structures within-case analysis of causal mechanisms using diagnostic evidence. Its explanatory logic differs from a population-level effect estimate.

Process tracing can examine how a proposed mechanism operates inside cases alongside a design estimating causal effects. Neither substitutes for the other's the result you set out to estimate or assumptions.

combo:case-study-multiple-sources.label: Build a case study from complementary evidence sources
combo:case-study-multiple-sources.why_combine: A case study is a bounded research design, not a single collection method. Interviews, documents and observation can reveal different sides of the same case. A survey or existing dataset can be added when the case question needs numerical evidence.
combo:case-study-multiple-sources.how_used: Define the case and question -> choose evidence sources that answer distinct parts -> collect and analyse each with its own method -> compare/integrate the sources -> report contradictions and gaps.
combo:case-study-multiple-sources.condition: Use multiple sources when each contributes distinct evidence about the bounded case and there is a plan to interpret them together.
combo:case-study-multiple-sources.limits: More sources do not guarantee better evidence; source access, quality, ethics and contradictions still need assessment.
combo:case-study-multiple-sources.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:convergent-survey-interview.label: Compare survey and interview evidence
combo:convergent-survey-interview.why_combine: Collect numerical and interview evidence around the same question when the learner needs to compare whether they agree, differ or illuminate different parts of the issue.
combo:convergent-survey-interview.how_used: Plan the shared question and separate strands -> collect/analyse each appropriately -> compare or integrate results -> explain agreement, disagreement and remaining uncertainty.
combo:convergent-survey-interview.condition: Choose this only when there is a planned integration question, not merely because both methods are available.
combo:convergent-survey-interview.limits: Different samples, measures or timing may explain disagreement; convergence does not automatically prove truth.
combo:convergent-survey-interview.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:document-and-interview-elicitation.label: Use documents to support an interview
combo:document-and-interview-elicitation.why_combine: A document, timeline or participant-created record can help an interview explore how its author understands a decision or experience, rather than treating the document as self-explanatory.
combo:document-and-interview-elicitation.how_used: Select an appropriate document -> assess provenance and sensitivity -> invite the participant to interpret it -> analyse the document and account separately, then connect them.
combo:document-and-interview-elicitation.condition: Useful when the document has meaning to a participant or records a process the interview asks about.
combo:document-and-interview-elicitation.limits: One person's interpretation does not establish the document's complete provenance or institutional meaning.
combo:document-and-interview-elicitation.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:explanatory-sequential.label: Measure a pattern, then explain it
combo:explanatory-sequential.why_combine: A survey can show which patterns are common in the sampled group. Follow-up interviews can explore how participants understand or experience a surprising or important pattern.
combo:explanatory-sequential.how_used: Survey -> identify a result needing explanation -> select interview participants/questions -> analyse interviews -> integrate the explanation with the survey findings.
combo:explanatory-sequential.condition: Choose this when the numerical result needs context or an explanation that the survey did not collect.
combo:explanatory-sequential.limits: Interviews explain meanings and mechanisms; they do not independently prove why the survey pattern occurred or make the survey causal.
combo:explanatory-sequential.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:exploratory-sequential.label: Explore first, measure next
combo:exploratory-sequential.why_combine: Use interviews or focus groups to discover local language, experiences or response options, then build a survey to examine how widely those patterns appear. The first phase informs the second. The two are not just separate studies placed together.
combo:exploratory-sequential.how_used: Qualitative inquiry -> refine concepts/questions -> pilot the survey -> collect and analyse survey data -> explain how the phases connect.
combo:exploratory-sequential.condition: Choose this when the topic or likely answer range is not yet understood well enough to design useful survey items.
combo:exploratory-sequential.limits: A small qualitative phase does not estimate prevalence; a later survey is only generalisable to the extent its sampling and measurement support that claim.
combo:exploratory-sequential.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:focus-group-to-survey.label: Use group discussion to shape a survey
combo:focus-group-to-survey.why_combine: Focus groups can reveal concepts, wording and response options participants use, helping a later questionnaire ask clearer and more relevant questions.
combo:focus-group-to-survey.how_used: Review the topic and evidence -> facilitate a bounded group discussion -> identify candidate concepts/language -> draft and cognitively test survey items -> pilot before wider use.
combo:focus-group-to-survey.condition: Useful when the researcher cannot confidently anticipate the range of answers or locally meaningful terms.
combo:focus-group-to-survey.limits: Group interaction can shape what people say; group findings do not establish how common a view is.
combo:focus-group-to-survey.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:interview-and-observation.label: Compare what people say with situated observation
combo:interview-and-observation.why_combine: Interviews provide accounts and interpretations. Observation can document actions, interactions and settings. Their comparison can expose context or differences between reported and observed practice.
combo:interview-and-observation.how_used: Frame the shared question -> conduct ethically appropriate interviews and observations -> keep distinct records -> compare what each source can show and explain divergence.
combo:interview-and-observation.condition: Use when understanding both accounts and situated practice matters and observation is permitted and feasible.
combo:interview-and-observation.limits: Observation is selective and may change behaviour; it cannot reveal private motives without additional evidence.
combo:interview-and-observation.selection_rule: Optional. Learner may select this combination only when the research question benefits from the stated integration. It does not make every constituent method compulsory across this field.

combo:participatory-method-choice.why_combine: Participatory research is a governance and collaboration approach. It can use interviews, group discussions, surveys or observation when participants and the question justify them.
combo:participatory-method-choice.how_used: Agree the question, roles and decision rights -> choose accessible evidence methods together -> collect/analyse with appropriate participation -> share interpretation and action decisions transparently.
combo:participatory-method-choice.condition: Use where the research purpose and governance genuinely involve participants in shaping decisions; do not label ordinary data collection participatory.
combo:participatory-method-choice.limits: Participation does not remove power imbalances, consent obligations, safety risks or the need to justify sampling and analysis.

combo:survey-followup-focus-group.label: Use group discussion to interpret survey findings
combo:survey-followup-focus-group.why_combine: A survey can identify a distribution or subgroup difference. A focus group can explore how participants interpret the issue and what explanations merit further investigation.
combo:survey-followup-focus-group.how_used: Analyse survey -> define the unresolved question -> recruit a purposeful discussion group -> analyse interaction and accounts -> connect the qualitative interpretation back to the survey limits.
combo:survey-followup-focus-group.condition: Choose when the survey surfaces an ambiguity that can be explored through group discussion.
combo:survey-followup-focus-group.limits: A focus group is not a representative vote and should not be used to estimate population percentages.

domain-emerging:d078-emerging-ai-assiste.label: AI-assisted annotation of social-research text, with human validation
domain-emerging:d078-emerging-ai-assiste.learner_output: A documented annotation dataset, codebook/label definitions, a human-reviewed error and subgroup check, and a short report explaining what labels can and cannot support.

works_with: task-specific validity, sensitivity and error analysis
alternatives: manual coding with a documented codebook
conventional NLP or supervised text-classification models when data, labels and task justify them

domain-emerging:d078-emerging-ai-assiste.what_it_is: A human-led workflow that uses an AI model to suggest labels or structured fields for text (for example, open survey answers, interview excerpts, policy documents or public posts), then checks the suggestions against a task-specific human-coded sample and the research construct.
limitations: Models can hallucinate, misunderstand local language and context, or make errors associated with participant characteristics. Aggregate accuracy alone can hide unequal errors.
A model's performance on one corpus, construct, language or model version does not establish performance elsewhere.
It cannot replace qualitative interpretation, informed consent, ethics review, or the researcher’s accountability for conclusions.
Sensitive or identifiable material must not be sent to a service without an approved data-handling basis.

domain-emerging:d078-experimental-synthe.label: Critically test AI-generated social responses or agents in exploratory simulations
domain-emerging:d078-experimental-synthe.learner_output: A simulation protocol with explicit agent assumptions, prompt/model/version and settings, scenario conditions, sensitivity checks, comparison against empirical or theoretical anchors, and a statement that the output is synthetic.

complements: empirical survey, interview, administrative or observational evidence where the research question requires human/population claims
preregistered or otherwise documented sensitivity analyses
alternatives: conventional agent-based simulation using explicit behavioral rules
pilot testing with actual participants when wording, comprehension or lived experience is the target

domain-emerging:d078-experimental-synthe.what_it_is: An experimental workflow that uses language-model-generated responses or agents to explore scenarios, test prompts, generate hypotheses, or examine whether an analytic procedure behaves as expected, then compares the results with theory and appropriate real-world evidence.
limitations: LLM-generated participants can flatten identity differences and misrepresent groups; mitigations do not necessarily remove this risk.
Outputs depend on model, prompts, settings and conditioning and may under-represent heterogeneity or important temporal dependencies.
Never treat generated participants as a replacement for real participants, probability samples, observed behavior or valid population inference.
This is not yet a routine, universally accepted social-research method; clearly label it experimental and obtain relevant ethics review.

domain-item:d078-agent-based-modeling.label: Agent-based modelling of social processes

requirement_scope.condition: Use agent-based modelling when a stated theory or mechanism can be represented as interacting agents and a simulation can help explore possible patterns; simulation output is not evidence that real people will behave that way.
requirement_scope.rationale: Agent-based modelling is used to explore how specified rules and interactions among simulated agents can produce patterns at a group or system level.

domain-item:d078-agent-based-modeling.requirement_reason: An optional focus for a narrower question. You can continue through Social Sciences without it. Select it when that work fits what you want to learn.

relationships.note: One modelling approach within computational social research, not a synonym for every computational method.
Mesa is one general-purpose Python framework for implementing an agent-based model; choose it only after the method and model assumptions are justified.
Casevo is a narrower cognitive-agent/network simulation option, not the default tool for agent-based modelling.

relationships.target: observational, survey, interview or statistical approaches
relationships.note: Use a simulation when the question concerns interactions or mechanisms that can be represented and explored; it does not replace empirical evidence.

limitations: A recognized specialist method, not a shared this field requirement.
The National Academies example is in hazards/disaster research; the NCRM learning resource targets advanced researchers.
Models depend on assumptions and need verification, validation, sensitivity analysis and clear documentation. Simulation output alone is not empirical confirmation.
Do not describe agent-based modelling as equivalent to all computational modelling.
domain-item:d078-agent-based-modeling.meaning: Agent-based modelling (ABM) is a computer simulation in which represented people, groups or organisations follow stated rules and interact. Researchers can explore how those interactions might produce wider patterns-for example, how communication rules could affect the spread of an idea. A simulation is a simplified model, not proof that real people will behave exactly that way.

domain-item:d078-confirmatory-factor-ana.label: Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)

requirement_scope.rationale: Test a theoretically specified latent measurement structure against observed item data. State identification and estimator choices, assess model fit and residuals, and evaluate measurement invariance before interpreting latent mean/group differences. A good fit alone does not prove construct validity.

domain-item:d078-confirmatory-factor-ana.meaning: Confirmatory factor analysis tests a measurement structure you specified in advance. State how the model is identified and which estimator you used. Judge fit and residuals. Check measurement invariance before you compare latent means across groups. A good fit does not, by itself, prove that the measure is valid.
domain-item:d078-confirmatory-factor-ana.learner_output: The prespecified model, the fit evidence, the uncertainty of the estimates, the diagnostics, and the scope of the claim.

domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.label: Conversation analysis (CA) of talk-in-interaction

requirement_scope.rationale: Study how participants organize naturally occurring interaction turn by turn, including turn-taking, sequence organization, repair and the actions accomplished through talk. Use recordings and sufficiently detailed transcripts, analyze cases closely, and ground claims in participants’ displayed orientations. CA is distinct from CDA and generic thematic coding.

domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.meaning: Conversation analysis studies how people organise talk, turn by turn, in a recording of real interaction. The evidence is the sequence: who speaks, how the next turn responds, and how repair happens. Claims should be grounded in what the participants treat as relevant. It is not the same as critical discourse analysis or a general theme code.
domain-item:d078-conversation-analysis.learner_output: An analysis tied to the transcript, with the sequential evidence and the transcription conventions. Automatic speech or text measures may help you find passages. They do not replace the sequential reading.

domain-item:d078-count-regression.label: Count regression: Poisson and negative binomial models

requirement_scope.rationale: Model non-negative event counts with exposure/offset and dependence structure represented appropriately. Start with Poisson when its mean-variance structure is plausible; consider negative binomial when overdispersion is supported, and diagnose zero inflation, clustering and excess zeros rather than selecting by habit.

domain-item:d078-count-regression.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-count-regression.meaning: Poisson and negative binomial models are for counts of events. Include the exposure, such as time or population at risk, when the design has one. Start with Poisson when its assumptions fit. Use the negative binomial when the counts vary more than Poisson expects. Check extra zeros and clustering rather than choosing a model by habit.
domain-item:d078-count-regression.learner_output: The model, the exposure, the dispersion checks, predicted rates or effects, and the uncertainty. The model does not create a causal result.
limitations: This optional item does not become compulsory by appearing on a route.

domain-item:d078-exploratory-factor-anal.label: Exploratory factor analysis (EFA)

requirement_scope.rationale: Explore plausible latent dimensions underlying a set of measured items when theory and prior evidence do not yet specify a sufficiently constrained structure. domain-item:d078-exploratory-factor-anal.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.

domain-item:d078-exponential-random-grap.label: Exponential-family random graph models (ERGMs)

requirement_scope.rationale: Model the probability of network configurations as a function of theoretically motivated structural and actor/covariate terms such as reciprocity, homophily and transitivity. Define the network boundary and tie process, assess convergence and goodness of fit, and interpret parameters as conditional network structure rather than independent observations.

domain-item:d078-exponential-random-grap.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-exponential-random-grap.meaning: An exponential-family random graph model estimates how likely a network pattern is, given terms such as reciprocity, similar actors being connected, and closed triangles. Define who is in the network and what counts as a tie. Check that the model converged and that it reproduces the patterns you care about. The estimates describe the network's structure. They do not treat each tie as an independent observation.
domain-item:d078-exponential-random-grap.learner_output: The network boundary, the model terms, the convergence and fit checks, and a bounded reading of the estimates.
limitations: This optional item does not become compulsory by appearing on a route.

domain-item:d078-fisher-exact-test.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-fisher-exact-test.meaning: Fisher's exact test looks for an association in a table of counts, especially a 2 by 2 table, when the usual chi-square approximation is not suitable. domain-item:d078-fisher-exact-test.learner_output: The table, the null hypothesis, an odds ratio where one applies, an interval, the exact procedure, and a bounded reading of the result. The test is about association, not cause.

domain-item:d078-regularized-linear-regr.label: Regularized linear regression: ridge, LASSO and elastic net

requirement_scope.rationale: Use penalized linear models when prediction or high-dimensional estimation makes unregularized OLS unstable: ridge shrinks coefficients, LASSO induces sparsity and elastic net combines penalties. Tune within training folds and prevent leakage; shrunken/selected coefficients are not ordinary unbiased OLS estimates.

domain-item:d078-regularized-linear-regr.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.

Tune the penalty inside the training data only. A shrunk coefficient is not the same kind of estimate as ordinary least squares.
domain-item:d078-regularized-linear-regr.learner_output: The penalty you chose, how you tuned it, the performance on kept-back data, and the limits of the selected coefficients. This is a prediction tool, not a causal design.

domain-item:d078-scikit-learn.requirement_reason: An optional focus for a narrower question. You can continue through Social Sciences without it. Select it when that work fits what you want to learn.
domain-item:d078-scikit-learn.learner_output: A documented, repeatable text- or table-analysis pipeline: the research question and labels. How data were prepared. Model and feature choices. Kept-back test data evaluation (for classification, for example, precision/recall and a confusion matrix). Error checks. And a statement of what the model can and cannot support.

relationships.note: Basic Python is needed to load data, call the library and inspect results.
pandas may prepare tables, labels and metadata before modelling.
It can implement selected text or predictive steps within a larger computational social-research design.
Error analysis, evidence appraisal and substantive theory are needed to interpret model output.

relationships.target: human coding, dictionary/rule-based coding, R tidymodels/quanteda or another justified workflow
relationships.note: Prediction is not automatically better than a transparent or interpretive alternative.

limitations: A model learns patterns in the examples and labels it receives. It does not decide whether a social concept was measured well, a label is fair, or a result is meaningful.

Good kept-back test data prediction does not establish causality, representativeness, construct validity, fairness or the truth of an interpretation. The study design and evidence still govern those claims.
Bag-of-words text features can discard word order and multi-word meaning. The official guide notes that this loses much of a document's internal structure.

English-only text features may miss local meanings in Nigerian Pidgin or code-mixed text. A 2020 Nigerian Pidgin sentiment study found that direct English sentiment analysis missed contextual meanings in its dataset. This is a bounded example, not a finding about every Nigerian language or task.

This candidate is conditional specialist software, not a shared this field foundation, a required library for every route, a professional credential, or evidence that a learner can independently conduct valid research.
Prediction alone does not establish explanation, causality, fairness or social validity.

domain-item:d078-spatial-autocorrelation.label: Spatial autocorrelation: Moran's I and local indicators (LISA)

requirement_scope.rationale: Measure global clustering and local spatial association after defining the spatial units, weights matrix and hypothesis. Use permutation/reference procedures and account for multiple local tests; the statistic identifies spatial pattern, not a mechanism or causal effect.

domain-item:d078-spatial-autocorrelation.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-spatial-autocorrelation.meaning: Moran's I and local indicators ask whether nearby places are more alike than you would expect by chance. Define the places, the weights that say who counts as a neighbour, and the hypothesis. Account for the fact that many local tests are run together. The statistic shows a spatial pattern. It does not name the mechanism or a cause.
domain-item:d078-spatial-autocorrelation.learner_output: The weights, the global and local statistics, the reference procedure, and a reading that keeps the scale and the boundaries in view.
limitations: This optional item does not become compulsory by appearing on a route.

domain-item:d078-spatial-regression-mode.label: Spatial regression: spatial lag and spatial error models

requirement_scope.rationale: Model spatial dependence or spatial heterogeneity when the research question, spatial weights and data support it. Distinguish outcome spillovers from correlated errors, test residual spatial dependence and interpret direct/indirect effects carefully; ordinary OLS is a baseline, not an automatic substitute.

domain-item:d078-spatial-regression-mode.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-spatial-regression-mode.meaning: Spatial lag and spatial error models are for dependence or unevenness across places. A lag model and an error model answer different questions: one is about spillover in the outcome, the other about correlated residuals. Test whether spatial pattern remains, and read direct and indirect effects carefully. Ordinary least squares is a baseline, not an automatic substitute.
domain-item:d078-spatial-regression-mode.learner_output: The weights, the model you chose and why, the checks, the effect reading, and the uncertainty.

domain-item:d078-tree-ensemble-predictio.label: Tree-ensemble machine learning for prediction and classification

requirement_scope.rationale: Use random forests or gradient-boosted trees for supervised prediction/classification when nonlinearities or interactions may improve held-out predictive performance. Compare against a simple, well-calibrated baseline; tune without leakage and report calibration, subgroup errors, uncertainty and explainability limits. These models do not replace inferential tests or causal identification.

domain-item:d078-tree-ensemble-predictio.meaning: Random forests and gradient-boosted trees can predict or classify when relationships are not a straight line. Compare them with a simple, well-calibrated baseline. Tune them without leaking test information. Report calibration, errors in subgroups, uncertainty, and how far the model can be explained. These models do not replace a statistical test or a causal design.
domain-item:d078-tree-ensemble-predictio.learner_output: A reproducible comparison with a baseline, kept-back test results, calibration and error notes, where the features and labels came from, and the limits.

domain-item:d078-wilcoxon-rank-tests.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum and signed-rank tests

requirement_scope.rationale: Use the rank-sum/Mann–Whitney procedure for two independent samples or the signed-rank procedure for paired observations when the target and design suit a rank-based comparison. These tests concern distributional/location contrasts under their assumptions; they are not automatic tests of medians and do not estimate the same quantity as every t-test.

domain-item:d078-wilcoxon-rank-tests.requirement_reason: Optional. This belongs to the method you selected. You can continue without choosing it.
domain-item:d078-wilcoxon-rank-tests.meaning: Use the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, also called Mann-Whitney, for two independent samples. Use the signed-rank test for paired observations. These tests compare rank or distribution patterns under their own assumptions. They are not automatic tests of medians, and they do not estimate the same quantity as every t-test.
domain-item:d078-wilcoxon-rank-tests.learner_output: A rank-test result labelled with the design, an effect or interval where the procedure supports one, notes on ties, and a cautious reading of the contrast.

domain-method:network-analysis.label: Network analysis
domain-method:network-analysis.plain_language_meaning: A family of methods for representing entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, then examining the resulting structure or patterns.
domain-method:network-analysis.meaning_in_domain: In this field, network analysis is relevant when relationships among people, organisations, places or digital entities are central to the question. Social network analysis is the social-science-focused branch when the nodes and ties represent social actors and relations.
domain-method:network-analysis.limitations: A network representation depends on boundary, node, tie, direction, time-window and missing-data decisions. Metrics describe the supplied graph. They do not establish causality or make a network representative.

domain-method:social-network-analysis.label: Social network analysis
domain-method:social-network-analysis.plain_language_meaning: A way to study relationships between people, groups or other social actors by defining who or what counts as a node and which connections count as ties, then analysing the resulting network.
domain-method:social-network-analysis.meaning_in_domain: In this field it is useful only when relationships themselves are part of the research question. It is not the same as analysing social-media content, and a graph picture alone does not establish a social finding.
domain-method:social-network-analysis.limitations: Requires a defensible network boundary, valid relational data and an explicit definition of each tie. Missing ties, platform access and sampling choices can change the apparent network. Network measures do not prove causation or personal importance.

domain:D078.label: Social Sciences & Behavioural Research
domain:D078.overview: Social Sciences helps you understand how people live together, how groups and institutions shape everyday life, and how societies change. It connects questions about culture, family, work, inequality, crime, policy and community life to evidence gathered through research. The field looks at individual behaviour as well as the relationships between people, institutions, the environment and wider social systems. Different disciplines study these questions from different viewpoints: Sociology is one route into Social Sciences, not another name for the whole field. In Nigeria, the NUC places Sociology alongside programmes such as Economics, Political Science and Psychology within Social Sciences. Researchers use concepts, comparison and evidence to describe patterns, examine explanations and consider social responses. What a particular study can conclude depends on its question, evidence and method.

overview_evidence.supports: Student-friendly illustration of social relationships and group life; not a definition of every Social Sciences discipline.

student_orientation.whatItStudies: You may study people, families, communities, culture, institutions, inequality, crime, work, politics and social change. The field looks at everyday experience and the wider systems that shape it.
student_orientation.whatPeopleDo: Depending on their work, people may study communities, institutions or social patterns; gather information through surveys, interviews, observation or records; analyse quantitative evidence (information expressed as numbers) or qualitative evidence (people’s words and explanations); and report what the evidence can and cannot show.
questions: How do families, communities and institutions shape people’s lives?
How do inequality, crime and other social problems develop, and how do people respond?
How do cultures, organisations and societies change over time?
What can evidence show about whether a policy or programme is working?
What patterns in social information reveal relationships among people, groups and institutions?
outputs: Research questions, proposals and study plans
Survey, interview, observation or fieldwork information
Research reports and explanations of findings
Recommendations when the evidence supports them
howWorkHappens: Begin with a question about people, groups, institutions or social change.
Choose a suitable approach, such as surveys, interviews, observation or document study; quantitative and qualitative approaches answer different kinds of questions.
Gather and handle information responsibly, considering consent, privacy, context and limitations.
Analyse the evidence and explain what it supports, what it does not show and what could be studied next.
student_orientation.whereProgrammeFits: In Nigeria’s NUC curriculum, Sociology is one programme within Social Sciences. Its curriculum covers social structure, culture, groups, institutions, inequality, crime, family, social problems, social change and research. Other Social Sciences programmes may examine overlapping questions from different perspectives.

programme-theme:sociology:african_societ.label: African and Nigerian societies
programme-theme:sociology:african_societ.description: These courses examine African and Nigerian social structures, cultures, histories and regional settings.
programme-theme:sociology:african_societ.narration: You will study the histories, cultures, languages, institutions and social organisation of Nigerian and other African societies. Regional examples help you compare how societies differ and change. They are not presented as one story that describes every community.

programme-theme:sociology:applied_practi.label: Social work and practical change
programme-theme:sociology:applied_practi.description: These courses connect social-science knowledge with social work, community services, innovation and practical responses to social needs.
programme-theme:sociology:applied_practi.narration: You will consider social causes of problems and the services and organisations that respond to them, then explore how social-science knowledge can support practical ideas and services. The curriculum’s examples are learning topics, not a guarantee of professional qualification.

programme-theme:sociology:governance.label: Politics and organisations
programme-theme:sociology:governance.description: These courses examine political life, collective action, formal organisations and how institutions work with society.
programme-theme:sociology:governance.narration: You will study how social conditions influence political activity, parties and movements, and how formal organisations are structured and operate. This connects institutions to the people and communities around them.

programme-theme:sociology:ideas.label: Ideas and foundations
programme-theme:sociology:ideas.description: Courses in this part introduce the concepts, history and theories used to make sense of the programme’s subject area.
programme-theme:sociology:ideas.narration: You will learn how Sociology developed, explore key concepts and compare sociological theories. The programme uses these ideas to help explain social institutions, relationships and change.

programme-theme:sociology:people.label: People, groups and society
programme-theme:sociology:people.description: Courses in this part help you examine the people, groups, institutions, cultures or systems named in the programme record.
programme-theme:sociology:people.narration: You will examine how people behave and relate to one another, and how families, groups, culture, language and social settings shape everyday life. The courses draw on Sociology, Anthropology and Psychology while keeping their different viewpoints distinct.

programme-theme:sociology:research.label: Research and evidence
programme-theme:sociology:research.description: Courses in this part show how the programme asks questions, gathers information, examines evidence and communicates findings.
programme-theme:sociology:research.narration: You will move from forming a research question and planning a study to choosing suitable methods, collecting and analysing information, and explaining what the evidence can-and cannot-show. The curriculum includes quantitative approaches, which work with numbers, and qualitative approaches, which examine words, experiences and meaning.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_communi.label: Communication and academic writing
programme-theme:sociology:shared_communi.description: Shared university learning in clear English, reading, writing, reasoning and presenting ideas.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_communi.narration: You will practise communicating clearly in speech and writing, understanding written information, and presenting ideas. These are shared university skills that support your Sociology studies. The course does not replace the discipline-specific research and reporting taught elsewhere in the programme.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_enterpr.label: Entrepreneurship and venture creation
programme-theme:sociology:shared_enterpr.description: Shared courses on identifying opportunities, developing ideas and understanding how ventures are planned.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_enterpr.narration: You will explore how people identify an unmet need, develop an idea and plan a possible venture. These shared courses introduce entrepreneurship and venture creation. They do not promise that an idea will succeed or replace Sociology's study of social and economic conditions.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_nigeria.label: Nigerian peoples and culture
programme-theme:sociology:shared_nigeria.description: A shared course on Nigerian peoples, history, culture and social life.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_nigeria.narration: You will study Nigerian peoples and cultures through historical and social examples. This shared course adds Nigerian context to your university learning. It is not a complete account of every community or a substitute for the Sociology programme's own African and Nigerian society courses.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_peace_c.label: Peace, conflict and security
programme-theme:sociology:shared_peace_c.description: A shared course introducing peace, conflict, security and ways people respond to conflict.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_peace_c.narration: You will learn key ways people describe peace, conflict and security, and consider how conflict can arise and be addressed. This shared course introduces broad concepts. The Sociology courses examine particular social institutions, inequalities and settings in greater depth.

programme-theme:sociology:shared_philoso.label: Philosophy and reasoning
programme-theme:sociology:shared_philoso.description: A shared course on philosophical questions, logic and clear reasoning.
programme-theme:sociology:shared_philoso.narration: You will examine philosophical questions and practise logic-checking whether reasons support a conclusion. These are shared reasoning foundations, while sociological theory and evidence are developed in the Sociology courses.

programme-theme:sociology:social_change.label: Social change and development
programme-theme:sociology:social_change.description: These courses explore how societies change, what shapes development and how those changes affect people and institutions.
programme-theme:sociology:social_change.narration: You will compare explanations of social change and development, then consider how economic, political and historical conditions affect families, institutions and communities. The curriculum includes African and Nigerian contexts as well as wider theories.

programme-theme:sociology:social_issues.label: Inequality, gender and social problems
programme-theme:sociology:social_issues.description: These courses examine inequality, gender relations, crime and other social problems, including their causes and effects.
programme-theme:sociology:social_issues.narration: You will examine how inequality and gender relations shape people’s opportunities, and how crime and other social problems affect communities. The courses compare explanations and responses rather than treating any single cause or solution as universal.

programme-theme:sociology:technology.label: Technology and information
programme-theme:sociology:technology.description: Courses in this part cover the digital applications and information practices recorded for the programme.
programme-theme:sociology:technology.narration: You will practise using a computer and common applications to create, organise and present information. The curriculum names these as general computing skills. It does not make a particular software brand a Sociology requirement.
